metadata.narrative: Our city council is considering a local child allowance or refundable child tax credit for families with low incomes, but some members want to put the money into job programs, TANF-style work requirements, or an EITC expansion instead. Can you help me understand what the evidence says about monthly cash for families with children? How should we weigh poverty reduction, food and housing hardship, parents’ work incentives, racial equity, children’s long-term mobility, and administrative pitfalls if we want a policy that is practical for a mid-sized city?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Local elected officials are essentially replaying a well-documented national debate, as seen when a Chicago alderman opposed a guaranteed-income pilot by arguing the city should instead spend on child care and "getting people back to work," while other council colleagues framed cash as the more dignified anti-poverty tool.
On poverty reduction, the strongest single body of evidence comes from the 2021 federal Child Tax Credit expansion, which made the credit fully refundable and paid half of it monthly.

Columbia University researchers calculated that this expansion cut child poverty by about 29 percent in December 2021 alone, translating into roughly 3 million fewer children in poverty, and other estimates show the overall child poverty rate falling from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, the largest one-year drop on record.

When the expansion lapsed, child poverty reverted to 12.4 percent, the largest single-year increase in poverty since the supplemental measure was created, demonstrating how quickly monthly cash gains can be reversed once withdrawn.

On food and housing hardship specifically, a separate strand of research on the prior safety net found that as states tightened Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) eligibility and caseloads fell, food insecurity and child homelessness both rose, with effects concentrated among single mothers.
Consistent with this, peer-reviewed analysis of the 2021 CTC expansion found it reduced poverty, food insecurity, and material hardship without producing the employment declines critics predicted.

On the specific worry that cash weakens parents' work incentives, the closest comparable federal program, the Earned Income Tax Credit, has a strong track record of increasing work among single mothers, accounting for more than half of the 1984-1996 rise in employment among that group, partly because it is tied to earnings and phases in with work.

The Child Tax Credit, by contrast, is not earnings-conditioned, yet Roll, Hamilton, and Chun's evaluation found the 2021 expansion did not reduce employment, and Stockton's SEED guaranteed-income pilot, which gave $500 a month with no strings attached, saw full-time employment rise from 28 percent to 40 percent among recipients over the first year.

That same Stockton pilot found recipients' ability to cover a $400 emergency expense without borrowing rose from 25 percent to 52 percent, suggesting unconditional cash can stabilize households enough to support job search and retention rather than undermine it.

On racial equity, the 2021 CTC's full refundability mattered enormously because prior versions excluded families with little or no earnings, who are disproportionately Black and Latino due to labor market discrimination and occupational segregation; child poverty fell 8.8 percentage points for Black children and 6.3 points for Latino children in 2021, and one analysis attributes a 6.2-percentage-point reduction in poverty among Black children, or about 686,000 children, to the expansion.

Reverting to the non-fully-refundable credit disproportionately harms families of color again, since an estimated 45 percent of Black children and 39 percent of Latino children do not receive the full credit under the current design.

On children's long-term mobility, a randomized trial called Baby's First Years found that infants of mothers receiving $333 a month, versus $20, showed more high-frequency brain activity linked to learning and thinking after just one year, providing causal evidence that income itself, not just correlated disadvantage, shapes early development.

A natural-experiment study exploiting the December-versus-January birth cutoff for tax benefits found that a roughly $1,300 infancy cash transfer raised young-adult earnings by 1 to 2 percent, with effects persisting into the early thirties, driven by higher test scores, fewer behavioral problems, and higher graduation rates, and the added tax revenue from those higher earnings exceeded the initial transfer's cost.

At a broader geographic level, Chetty, Hendren, Kline, and Saez found that localities with larger tax credits for the poor tend to have higher intergenerational income mobility, though they stress that segregation, school quality, and family structure explain more of the variation across cities than tax policy alone, a caution relevant to any single city's expectations.

Turning to the TANF-style work-requirement alternative some council members favor, TANF today reaches only about 21 of every 100 families in poverty, compared with 68 of 100 under its predecessor AFDC, spends only about 10 percent of funds on work, education, and training activities, and applies sanctions disproportionately to Black families.

A more skeptical, market-oriented assessment argues 1996 welfare reform's effects were more modest than either critics or supporters claimed, with poverty declines only partly attributable to the policy itself and small, mixed effects on children's later mobility, a useful counterweight suggesting work requirements alone are unlikely to be transformative in either direction.

Finally, administrative design will make or break a city program: take-up failures left substantial 2021 poverty reduction on the table because many eligible non-filing families didn't know about the credit or lacked internet access to a portal with no Spanish version, and the IRS itself had to pause its non-filer sign-up tool mid-season due to duplicate-filing confusion.

Cities must also anticipate benefit cliffs, since the same monthly cash could interact with SNAP, TANF, or Medicaid eligibility formulas, and federal demonstrations testing gradual benefit "ramps" instead of cliffs found no employment gains, largely due to the administrative cost of tracking monthly income and beneficiaries' confusion about complex rules.

Practically, most existing city-level guaranteed-income pilots have been funded through one-time federal relief or philanthropic dollars rather than ongoing tax revenue, are modest in scale, and researchers caution they mainly teach delivery lessons rather than proving a sustainable funding model for a fully expanded program.

Given this evidence, a mid-sized city considering a monthly child allowance should design it as fully refundable and disregarded for other means-tested benefit calculations, pair it with proactive non-filer outreach in multiple languages, expect modest but real work-incentive benefits rather than harm, and treat a job-program or EITC-only substitute as complementary rather than a full replacement, since neither has matched cash's documented gains in poverty reduction, hardship relief, and early childhood outcomes.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

budget_tokens_per_result.description: Maximum approximate tokens staged per result. Text is bounded at tokens × 5 characters and cut at the final line break before that boundary. Default 4096.

tools.name: commit_context

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

Local elected officials are essentially replaying a well-documented national debate, as seen when a Chicago alderman opposed a guaranteed-income pilot by arguing the city should instead spend on child care and "getting people back to work," while other council colleagues framed cash as the more dignified anti-poverty tool.

On poverty reduction, the strongest single body of evidence comes from the 2021 federal Child Tax Credit expansion, which made the credit fully refundable and paid half of it monthly.

Columbia University researchers calculated that this expansion cut child poverty by about 29 percent in December 2021 alone, translating into roughly 3 million fewer children in poverty, and other estimates show the overall child poverty rate falling from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, the largest one-year drop on record. [shard_04482_60336] [shard_06531_26790]

When the expansion lapsed, child poverty reverted to 12.4 percent, the largest single-year increase in poverty since the supplemental measure was created, demonstrating how quickly monthly cash gains can be reversed once withdrawn. [shard_03612_32703]

On food and housing hardship specifically, a separate strand of research on the prior safety net found that as states tightened Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) eligibility and caseloads fell, food insecurity and child homelessness both rose, with effects concentrated among single mothers. [shard_03797_6398]

Consistent with this, peer-reviewed analysis of the 2021 CTC expansion found it reduced poverty, food insecurity, and material hardship without producing the employment declines critics predicted. [shard_03862_45785]

On the specific worry that cash weakens parents' work incentives, the closest comparable federal program, the Earned Income Tax Credit, has a strong track record of increasing work among single mothers, accounting for more than half of the 1984-1996 rise in employment among that group, partly because it is tied to earnings and phases in with work. [shard_03765_84554]

The Child Tax Credit, by contrast, is not earnings-conditioned, yet Roll, Hamilton, and Chun's evaluation found the 2021 expansion did not reduce employment, and Stockton's SEED guaranteed-income pilot, which gave $500 a month with no strings attached, saw full-time employment rise from 28 percent to 40 percent among recipients over the first year. [shard_03862_45785] [shard_03944_24468]

That same Stockton pilot found recipients' ability to cover a $400 emergency expense without borrowing rose from 25 percent to 52 percent, suggesting unconditional cash can stabilize households enough to support job search and retention rather than undermine it. [shard_03944_24468]

On racial equity, the 2021 CTC's full refundability mattered enormously because prior versions excluded families with little or no earnings, who are disproportionately Black and Latino due to labor market discrimination and occupational segregation; child poverty fell 8.8 percentage points for Black children and 6.3 points for Latino children in 2021, and one analysis attributes a 6.2-percentage-point reduction in poverty among Black children, or about 686,000 children, to the expansion. [shard_06531_26790] [shard_00588_78803]

Reverting to the non-fully-refundable credit disproportionately harms families of color again, since an estimated 45 percent of Black children and 39 percent of Latino children do not receive the full credit under the current design. [shard_06531_26790]

On children's long-term mobility, a randomized trial called Baby's First Years found that infants of mothers receiving $333 a month, versus $20, showed more high-frequency brain activity linked to learning and thinking after just one year, providing causal evidence that income itself, not just correlated disadvantage, shapes early development. [shard_00948_4211]

A natural-experiment study exploiting the December-versus-January birth cutoff for tax benefits found that a roughly $1,300 infancy cash transfer raised young-adult earnings by 1 to 2 percent, with effects persisting into the early thirties, driven by higher test scores, fewer behavioral problems, and higher graduation rates, and the added tax revenue from those higher earnings exceeded the initial transfer's cost. [shard_03548_31110]

At a broader geographic level, Chetty, Hendren, Kline, and Saez found that localities with larger tax credits for the poor tend to have higher intergenerational income mobility, though they stress that segregation, school quality, and family structure explain more of the variation across cities than tax policy alone, a caution relevant to any single city's expectations. [shard_06401_84175]

Turning to the TANF-style work-requirement alternative some council members favor, TANF today reaches only about 21 of every 100 families in poverty, compared with 68 of 100 under its predecessor AFDC, spends only about 10 percent of funds on work, education, and training activities, and applies sanctions disproportionately to Black families. [shard_03292_42809]

A more skeptical, market-oriented assessment argues 1996 welfare reform's effects were more modest than either critics or supporters claimed, with poverty declines only partly attributable to the policy itself and small, mixed effects on children's later mobility, a useful counterweight suggesting work requirements alone are unlikely to be transformative in either direction. [shard_04758_69514]

Finally, administrative design will make or break a city program: take-up failures left substantial 2021 poverty reduction on the table because many eligible non-filing families didn't know about the credit or lacked internet access to a portal with no Spanish version, and the IRS itself had to pause its non-filer sign-up tool mid-season due to duplicate-filing confusion. [shard_04482_60336] [shard_04945_76910]

Cities must also anticipate benefit cliffs, since the same monthly cash could interact with SNAP, TANF, or Medicaid eligibility formulas, and federal demonstrations testing gradual benefit "ramps" instead of cliffs found no employment gains, largely due to the administrative cost of tracking monthly income and beneficiaries' confusion about complex rules. [shard_02791_55589] [shard_00119_42893]

Practically, most existing city-level guaranteed-income pilots have been funded through one-time federal relief or philanthropic dollars rather than ongoing tax revenue, are modest in scale, and researchers caution they mainly teach delivery lessons rather than proving a sustainable funding model for a fully expanded program. [shard_03744_55131]

Given this evidence, a mid-sized city considering a monthly child allowance should design it as fully refundable and disregarded for other means-tested benefit calculations, pair it with proactive non-filer outreach in multiple languages, expect modest but real work-incentive benefits rather than harm, and treat a job-program or EITC-only substitute as complementary rather than a full replacement, since neither has matched cash's documented gains in poverty reduction, hardship relief, and early childhood outcomes. [shard_03765_84554] [shard_03292_42809]

answer.text: Local elected officials are essentially replaying a well-documented national debate, as seen when a Chicago alderman opposed a guaranteed-income pilot by arguing the city should instead spend on child care and "getting people back to work," while other council colleagues framed cash as the more dignified anti-poverty tool.
On poverty reduction, the strongest single body of evidence comes from the 2021 federal Child Tax Credit expansion, which made the credit fully refundable and paid half of it monthly.

Columbia University researchers calculated that this expansion cut child poverty by about 29 percent in December 2021 alone, translating into roughly 3 million fewer children in poverty, and other estimates show the overall child poverty rate falling from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, the largest one-year drop on record.

When the expansion lapsed, child poverty reverted to 12.4 percent, the largest single-year increase in poverty since the supplemental measure was created, demonstrating how quickly monthly cash gains can be reversed once withdrawn.

On food and housing hardship specifically, a separate strand of research on the prior safety net found that as states tightened Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) eligibility and caseloads fell, food insecurity and child homelessness both rose, with effects concentrated among single mothers.
Consistent with this, peer-reviewed analysis of the 2021 CTC expansion found it reduced poverty, food insecurity, and material hardship without producing the employment declines critics predicted.

On the specific worry that cash weakens parents' work incentives, the closest comparable federal program, the Earned Income Tax Credit, has a strong track record of increasing work among single mothers, accounting for more than half of the 1984-1996 rise in employment among that group, partly because it is tied to earnings and phases in with work.

The Child Tax Credit, by contrast, is not earnings-conditioned, yet Roll, Hamilton, and Chun's evaluation found the 2021 expansion did not reduce employment, and Stockton's SEED guaranteed-income pilot, which gave $500 a month with no strings attached, saw full-time employment rise from 28 percent to 40 percent among recipients over the first year.

That same Stockton pilot found recipients' ability to cover a $400 emergency expense without borrowing rose from 25 percent to 52 percent, suggesting unconditional cash can stabilize households enough to support job search and retention rather than undermine it.

On racial equity, the 2021 CTC's full refundability mattered enormously because prior versions excluded families with little or no earnings, who are disproportionately Black and Latino due to labor market discrimination and occupational segregation; child poverty fell 8.8 percentage points for Black children and 6.3 points for Latino children in 2021, and one analysis attributes a 6.2-percentage-point reduction in poverty among Black children, or about 686,000 children, to the expansion.

Reverting to the non-fully-refundable credit disproportionately harms families of color again, since an estimated 45 percent of Black children and 39 percent of Latino children do not receive the full credit under the current design.

On children's long-term mobility, a randomized trial called Baby's First Years found that infants of mothers receiving $333 a month, versus $20, showed more high-frequency brain activity linked to learning and thinking after just one year, providing causal evidence that income itself, not just correlated disadvantage, shapes early development.

A natural-experiment study exploiting the December-versus-January birth cutoff for tax benefits found that a roughly $1,300 infancy cash transfer raised young-adult earnings by 1 to 2 percent, with effects persisting into the early thirties, driven by higher test scores, fewer behavioral problems, and higher graduation rates, and the added tax revenue from those higher earnings exceeded the initial transfer's cost.

At a broader geographic level, Chetty, Hendren, Kline, and Saez found that localities with larger tax credits for the poor tend to have higher intergenerational income mobility, though they stress that segregation, school quality, and family structure explain more of the variation across cities than tax policy alone, a caution relevant to any single city's expectations.

Turning to the TANF-style work-requirement alternative some council members favor, TANF today reaches only about 21 of every 100 families in poverty, compared with 68 of 100 under its predecessor AFDC, spends only about 10 percent of funds on work, education, and training activities, and applies sanctions disproportionately to Black families.

A more skeptical, market-oriented assessment argues 1996 welfare reform's effects were more modest than either critics or supporters claimed, with poverty declines only partly attributable to the policy itself and small, mixed effects on children's later mobility, a useful counterweight suggesting work requirements alone are unlikely to be transformative in either direction.

Finally, administrative design will make or break a city program: take-up failures left substantial 2021 poverty reduction on the table because many eligible non-filing families didn't know about the credit or lacked internet access to a portal with no Spanish version, and the IRS itself had to pause its non-filer sign-up tool mid-season due to duplicate-filing confusion.

Cities must also anticipate benefit cliffs, since the same monthly cash could interact with SNAP, TANF, or Medicaid eligibility formulas, and federal demonstrations testing gradual benefit "ramps" instead of cliffs found no employment gains, largely due to the administrative cost of tracking monthly income and beneficiaries' confusion about complex rules.

Practically, most existing city-level guaranteed-income pilots have been funded through one-time federal relief or philanthropic dollars rather than ongoing tax revenue, are modest in scale, and researchers caution they mainly teach delivery lessons rather than proving a sustainable funding model for a fully expanded program.

Given this evidence, a mid-sized city considering a monthly child allowance should design it as fully refundable and disregarded for other means-tested benefit calculations, pair it with proactive non-filer outreach in multiple languages, expect modest but real work-incentive benefits rather than harm, and treat a job-program or EITC-only substitute as complementary rather than a full replacement, since neither has matched cash's documented gains in poverty reduction, hardship relief, and early childhood outcomes.
